analysis.one_liner: Nullifies a Labor Department rule that would extend overtime pay to millions of salaried workers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 202 cosponsors, all Republicans, but never got a committee vote or floor action before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2015 the Labor Department proposed redefining which salaried workers can be denied overtime under federal wage law. The proposed cutoff was more than double the one then in effect, so millions of salaried workers earning under it would become eligible for overtime pay or a salary raise. This bill would cancel that rule outright, wipe out any back-pay claims under it, bar the department from updating the salary cutoff automatically in the future, and require a long list of new economic studies before the department could issue anything like it again.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who pay salaried workers between the old cutoff and the new one — retail chains, restaurants, health care providers, nonprofits, and small businesses — would avoid paying overtime or raising salaries for workers they currently classify as exempt managers. The bill's own findings list small businesses, nonprofits, Medicare- and Medicaid-dependent health care providers, and small governments as the parties seeking relief.

how_it_helps.text: It cancels the Labor Department's proposed overtime rule, and if it had already become final, restores the old regulations as if it never took effect.
It would bar employees from suing employers for failing to comply with the rule before the bill's enactment, eliminating back-pay liability.
It forbids any future salary-threshold update from happening automatically; every change would need a fresh notice-and-comment rulemaking, a process that typically takes well over a year.

It requires a detailed economic analysis — disaggregated by state, industry, small business, nonprofit, school district, and health care provider — plus a 120-day comment period and an effective date at least one year out, before any substantially similar rule could be issued.

analysis.who_pays: Salaried workers earning between the old cutoff and the new one would stay exempt from overtime, meaning no extra pay for hours worked beyond 40 a week and no employer pressure to raise their salaries to keep them exempt.

drawbacks.text: Workers earning below the new cutoff would remain exempt from overtime protections, so hours beyond 40 a week would go unpaid for this group.

Because automatic updates are banned and every threshold change requires a full new rulemaking, the salary cutoff would drift far behind inflation over time, steadily shrinking the group protected by overtime law.
The bill would void liability for conduct before enactment, so employers who had underpaid workers under the old classification could not be made whole under the rule.

The bill's findings argue the rule was poorly analyzed — the Small Business Administration's Office of Advocacy said the department failed to identify how many small entities were affected and ignored regional cost-of-living differences — which supporters would cite as the cost an honest backer of the rule should acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains flow entirely to employers facing a labor-cost increase, while the loss falls on salaried workers who would keep working overtime without extra pay. The compliance-analysis provisions are written so broadly that reissuing a similar rule would take years, effectively locking in the old low threshold. The department's cost estimates were contested in the record, but the bill does not adjust the rule's level — it eliminates it and restricts the agency's ability to try again.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2016 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote after the committee referral.
It attracted 202 cosponsors, every one of them a Republican.
The bill targeted the Labor Department's proposed overtime rule, which its findings said would raise the exempt-salary threshold by 113 percent in its first year.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of salaried workers earning between the old and new salary cutoffs — retail, restaurant, health care, and small-business employers — are better off, because the bill that would have shielded them from the overtime rule died without a vote. Workers in that pay band keep their chance at overtime coverage, since the nullification never became law.

for.name: Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the Labor Department's overtime rule.

for.name: John Kline
for.role: Chairman, House Committee on Education and the Workforce; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined as the original cosponsor; his committee received the bill and never acted on it.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: His Labor Department proposed and finalized the overtime rule the bill sought to nullify, and his administration opposed congressional nullification of it.

sides.party_line_note: All 202 cosponsors were Republicans and none were Democrats, and the bill was introduced by two Republican members of the committee that controlled its fate.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurant, and other employers of salaried store and shift managers
industries.note: These employers rely on classifying low-paid salaried workers as exempt managers to avoid overtime. Nullifying the rule lets them keep that classification, which is the public's cost of the bill's benefit to them.

The bill was written around their claimed compliance burden, and its findings quote the Small Business Administration's Office of Advocacy criticizing the rule's small-entity analysis. Their gain is avoiding wage costs that would otherwise go to workers.

industries.industry: Medicare- and Medicaid-dependent health care providers
industries.note: The bill singles these providers out for special analysis before any similar rule could be issued, since the overtime expansion would have raised their payroll costs for salaried nursing and supervisory staff.

industries.industry: Small state and local governments, including school districts
industries.note: Listed in the bill as employers needing protection from the rule's salary threshold, whose avoidance of that cost comes out of potential pay for salaried public employees.
